cold: They can't climb. That was the rule.
d01: Day one. The Sea Empress. The biggest cruise ship in the world, three days out of Miami.
And you're carrying forty glasses across the pool deck when a man in a Hawaiian shirt bites the captain.
Six minutes later, the pool party is something else.
You drop the glasses. You run. Up a ladder, through a door marked Crew Only, onto the bridge.
d02: Day two. You wake up on the floor of the bridge. Someone is sitting in the captain's chair.
It's a cat. Orange. Wearing a tiny captain's hat. Her collar says Anchor.
The radio is static. The autopilot is still on, steering five thousand passengers toward nowhere at twenty knots.
The captain's real hat is on the floor. You put it on. It's too big.
d03: Day three. You're hungry, and the buffet never closes.
Deck fifteen, six A.M. A man in a bathrobe is still standing at the omelet station, waiting for his order.
You fill a room service cart. Bacon. Pancakes. Forty little jars of jam.
Halfway back, one wheel starts to squeak.
Every bathrobe in the room turns around.
You have never pushed a cart that fast in your life.
d04: Day four. You learn the first rule from a cat.
Anchor walks across the control panel and steps on the horn.
The sound is enormous. And every one of them, on every deck, turns toward it, and runs.
To the bow. They pile up against the railing, and the front row goes over the side.
And you're standing next to the loudest button on the ocean.
d05: Day five. Sports deck. You're looking for sunscreen when they find you.
Twenty of them. Nowhere to run but up.
So you go up the climbing wall, faster than anyone in the history of the Sea Empress.
At the top, you look down. They're reaching. Scratching. Falling off the first hold.
That night, you pull up the ladder to the bridge. Home.
d06: Day six. Nine P.M. The radio finally says something.
Anybody out there? This is Dolores. Key West.
She's seventy-one. A retired Navy radio operator with a bad hip and a beagle named Biscuit.
Every port is closed to infected ships, she says. Nobody's coming. But I'm not going anywhere either.
Stay on that bridge, kid. Talk to me every night at nine.
d07: Day seven. One week alive deserves a party.
At dawn, you tap the horn. Five thousand passengers run to the bow. And the pool deck is yours.
Breakfast: the chocolate fountain. Lunch: every flavor in the ice cream machine.
Dinner: lobster, in a bathrobe, in the hot tub.
Anchor eats the lobster. Fair enough.
Tonight, you're the only first-class passenger on the ocean.
d08: Day eight. The Boardwalk. A carousel, a candy shop, and a zip line across nine decks of open air.
You've been too scared to ride it all summer. Tonight, nobody's watching.
You scream the whole way down. Quietly.
Then the casino. You hit the jackpot on the first try.
One million dollars, and nobody left to pay you.
Remember the zip line. You'll need it.
d09: Day nine. Two waterslides, three hundred feet of twisting tube, and a pool at the bottom with nobody in it.
You go down forty-one times. Anchor watches every one. Unimpressed.
At sunset, you start the giant outdoor screen with the sound off, and play a cartoon.
On the deck below, three hundred faces turn up to the light.
They watch until the end. Nobody laughs.
d10: Day ten. Four A.M. The engines stop.
The lights die, deck by deck, until the whole ship is dark.
For the first time, you can hear the ocean. And five thousand footsteps.
The bridge still has one emergency battery. It runs the radio. And the horn.
One hundred percent. Every night with Dolores costs you three.
d11: Day eleven. The ship is dead in the water, and the sea is flat as glass.
At the stern, behind a door marked Marina, there are six jet skis nobody will ever rent again.
You take one out. You fall off twice. Then you get it.
Laps around the biggest ship in the world, at sunrise, with dolphins racing you.
For twenty minutes, you forget everything.
d12: Day twelve. You write a letter. Dear Mom. Dear Max. Don't worry. I'm the captain now.
Max is eight. He made you take his walkie-talkie, in case the ship sinks.
Range: two miles. You're four hundred miles from Miami.
You put the letter in a bottle. You don't notice you're crying until Anchor headbutts your chin.
Then: bang. A face hits the little window in the bridge door. The glass holds.
d13: Day thirteen. The buffet has started to smell.
Real food is on deck two, in the crew storerooms, at the end of a corridor the crew calls I-ninety-five.
You go down with a flashlight and the captain's keycard. Canned peaches. Rice. Crackers.
And the kitchen crew. Still in their white hats.
You get out through the escape trunk, a ladder up fourteen decks. They can't follow. You check.
d14: Day fourteen. Midnight. Lights on the horizon. A cargo ship, three miles away.
You flash the captain's flashlight. Three short. Three long. Three short. Over and over.
You try Max's walkie-talkie. Two-mile range. Static.
The lights keep going. They get smaller. Then they're gone.
On the radio, Dolores is quiet for a long time. Nobody stops for an infected ship, kid. Not yet.
d15: Day fifteen. Halfway. You have a routine.
Seven: push-ups on the helipad. Nine: you mop the bridge, because you're still the busboy.
Noon: fishing off the stern. Anchor steals the fish.
Six: you climb the funnel to watch the sunset, next to the old brass emergency horn with a pull chain.
Nine: Dolores. She's teaching you chess over the radio. You're terrible.
d16: Day sixteen. Eight P.M. There's a knock at the bridge door.
Through the little window: a white uniform. Gold stripes. It's the captain.
For twenty years, he started his watch on this bridge every night at eight. He still remembers.
Anchor runs to the door and purrs. She doesn't understand.
You keep the door shut. She sleeps against it every night after that.
d17: Day seventeen. The taps cough, then stop. No power, no fresh water. The pools are seawater.
Then, at noon, the sky goes dark, and it pours.
You run along the pool deck, turning every umbrella upside down. Buckets. Ice coolers. Your mouth.
Then you stand in the rain and laugh, until a whole deck of faces turns your way.
d18: Day eighteen. Anchor is gone. Not on the bridge. Not on the funnel. Not in the hot tub.
You find her eight decks down, asleep on the Boardwalk carousel, on a painted horse. Surrounded.
So you do the one thing every cat on Earth answers to. You open a can of tuna.
Anchor comes running. So does everybody else.
You have never climbed a ladder that fast.
d19: Day nineteen. Today, Max turns nine.
At nine P.M., Dolores does something she's not supposed to do. She patches the radio into a phone line. To Miami.
There's a click. Then: Leo? Baby? It's Mom.
Max grabs the phone and asks if you've seen any sharks.
You sing him happy birthday, very quietly, on the bridge of a dead ship. Mom cries. You don't. Almost.
d20: Day twenty. Dolores has news, and she says it slowly.
On day thirty, the Navy clears the shipping lanes. Every drifting infected ship gets sunk. No exceptions.
Unless someone aboard is alive, and they know exactly where it is.
The GPS died with the power. The Sea Empress has been drifting for ten days.
You don't know where you are. Nobody does.
d21: Day twenty-one. Dolores used to be a Navy navigator. Before satellites, she says, sailors found their way with this.
In the captain's cabin, behind glass: a brass sextant.
All night, she teaches you. The horizon. The North Star. Angles, tables, the math you swore you'd never need.
On the fifth try, you have it. Twenty-six north. Seventy-four west.
Dolores whistles. That's Navy grade, Captain.
d22: A Coast Guard cutter, the Valiant, will reach you at dawn on day thirty.
They won't board an infected ship. You'll have to come to them.
So you make a plan. The horn sends them all to the bow. The zip line drops you to the Boardwalk.
Run to the stern. Jet ski. Go.
You walk the route every night. Forty-one seconds.
d23: Day twenty-three. The sky in the south turns a color you've never seen. Green.
Dolores sounds scared for the first time. Hurricane Ivy. Category four. Coming right at you.
You tie down everything on the bridge.
You find the smallest life vest on the ship, from the kids' club, and put it on Anchor.
She hates it. You tell her she looks very professional.
d24: Day twenty-four. Ivy hits at midnight.
The biggest ship in the world rolls like a bath toy. Deck chairs fly by the hundred. The waterslides snap.
Hundreds of them slide across the deck and go over the rail, one wave at a time.
On the bridge, you hold the wheel with one arm and Anchor with the other.
And you scream with the wind, because for once, nobody can hear you.
d25: Day twenty-five. Morning. The storm is gone. So is the radio antenna.
No antenna, no Dolores. And no way to tell the Valiant where you are.
The spare is at the top of the radar mast. Sixty feet up, on a ship that still rolls.
You climb. You don't look down. You fix it.
The first voice you hear is Dolores, crying. Kid. I thought I'd lost you.
d26: Day twenty-six. The storm pushed you two hundred miles north. You take a new fix with the sextant. Dolores passes it on.
Then, at sunset, you see something on the sports deck that makes your stomach drop.
They're at the climbing wall. On top of each other. A pile of bodies, higher every minute.
The one on top touches the last hold.
They can't climb. But they're learning.
d27: Day twenty-seven. Battery: four percent. Enough for one last call, and one blast of the horn.
You tell Dolores everything. The plan. The forty-one seconds. Max's walkie-talkie.
If I don't make it, you say. Don't, kid, she says. You'll make it. I want to meet that cat.
That night, there's scratching under the bridge wing. And it's getting higher.
d28: Day twenty-eight. Midnight. They come up the side of the bridge, on each other's shoulders.
A hand grabs your ankle. You kick. It lets go.
You grab Anchor and the walkie-talkie, and you go up, through the roof hatch.
Behind you, they pour onto the bridge. The radio. The battery. The horn button. All of it, gone.
You crawl along the cable to the funnel, in the rain, and you don't let go.
d29: Day twenty-nine. The top of the funnel, the highest point on the ship. Below you, every deck is crawling.
No radio. No food. Half a bottle of water, which you share with a cat.
Next to you is the old brass horn. No power needed. Just a chain.
At the bottom of the climbing wall, they're stacking again. Higher.
You sit with your hand on the chain, and you wait for the sun.
d30: Day thirty. Dawn. A white ship on the horizon.
Max's walkie-talkie crackles. Two-mile range. Sea Empress, this is the cutter Valiant. Anybody aboard?
You pull the chain. The horn screams. Five thousand heads turn to the bow.
You zip-line over the Boardwalk, run for the stern, and hit the water on a jet ski, Anchor inside your vest.
epi: Key West. Dolores is shorter than you thought. Biscuit loves Anchor. Anchor does not love Biscuit.
And on Miami Beach, a bottle washes up. Dear Mom. I'm the captain now.
